findings.title: Device-limit denial is cached, so a retry is allowed
findings.body: tagDeviceUI writes the device cache key (29-minute TTL) before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, that error is now propagated and Anonymous.Authenticate denies the request, but the cache entry is left in place. The next TagDevice call for the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, returns nil, and anonymous authentication succeeds even though the device was never stored. After one rejection per process, the configured limit is not enforced for the rest of the TTL; the new store test never calls TagDevice twice, so it does not catch this.

findings.title: Omitting the device ID header skips the limit and still grants anonymous access
findings.body: The new limit is enforced only inside TagDevice, and TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing. Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity with the configured org role. The header is client-supplied, so any caller can keep using anonymous auth after device_limit is exhausted by simply not sending it (or by rotating IDs until the cache bypass above applies). The cap does not actually bound anonymous access.

findings.title: Device limit check and insert are not atomic
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one session, then inserts in another, with no transaction, row lock, or advisory lock. Concurrent anonymous requests (including across HA instances, which do not share the in-process cache) can all observe count < device_limit and all insert. Nothing in the schema caps the number of rows, so the overshoot sticks: active devices refresh updated_at about every 29 minutes and never fall out of the 30-day window used by the count. The limit can be permanently exceeded until those extra devices go idle for 30 days.

findings.title: Anonymous auth now waits on device tagging even when the limit is off
findings.body: Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with a detached 2-minute timeout and a panic recover, so it could not stall authentication. It is now a synchronous TagDevice call on the request context for every anonymous login, including the default device_limit of 0 (unlimited), which still does a database upsert on each cache miss. A slow or stuck database delays or ties up all anonymous requests until the DB call returns or the request is cancelled; a panic in tagging is no longer isolated from the request.

findings.title: Provider signature change is not matched by Wire
findings.body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit parameter. Grafana constructs these via the committed Wire graph (pkg/server/wire.go / wire_gen.go), which is not updated in this PR. wire_gen.go still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile until Wire is regenerated and the generated file is included.

findings.title: Limit test never covers auth, cache, or an existing device
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a second new device ID is rejected by the store. It does not check that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated when count == device_limit, and nothing in impl_test or the auth client tests asserts that a second TagDevice/Authenticate after ErrDeviceLimitReached stays denied. Those are the paths that actually decide whether anonymous users are blocked, and both currently fail open.
